cards.front: What is the main difference between ionic, covalent, and metallic bonding?
cards.back: **Electron behavior** differs. Ionic bonding transfers electrons between atoms. Covalent bonding shares electron pairs between particular atoms. Metallic bonding lets electrons move throughout the metal.
cards.hint: Think about where the electrons end up.

cards.front: How does an electronegativity difference predict how electrons are shared in a bond?
cards.back: A small difference gives a **nonpolar covalent** bond with fairly equal sharing. A larger difference between nonmetals gives a **polar covalent** bond, with electron density closer to the more electronegative atom.
cards.hint: Ask which atom pulls the shared electrons harder.

cards.front: Why does solid metal conduct electricity but a solid ionic compound does not?
cards.back: **Delocalized electrons** can move through solid metal and carry charge. In a solid ionic compound, the ions cannot move freely, so there are no mobile charged particles.
cards.hint: Name the mobile charged particle in each case.

cards.back: An **electrical attraction** that holds atoms or ions together.
cards.hint: What force holds the particles together?

cards.back: How **strongly an atom attracts electrons** in a chemical bond.
cards.hint: Think about pulling power for electrons.

cards.back: The **attraction** between positive metal ions and delocalized electrons throughout the metal.
cards.hint: Which particles are attracted to which?

cards.back: Electrons that **move throughout a metal** rather than belonging to one atom or bond.
cards.hint: Contrast them with electrons in a single covalent bond.

cards.back: **Discrete groups of atoms** held together by covalent bonds.
cards.hint: Covalent bonds hold the atoms together.

cards.front: A student says a polar covalent bond means the electrons are fully transferred to one atom. What is wrong?
cards.back: **Unequal sharing is not complete transfer.** A polar covalent bond still has shared electrons, with density closer to the more electronegative atom.

cards.front: A student says all covalent substances have low melting points and all ionic compounds always conduct. What is wrong?
cards.back: These are **useful patterns, not universal rules**. Some covalent substances form networks with very high melting points. Solid ionic compounds do not conduct because their ions cannot move freely.
cards.hint: Look for how general the claims are.

cards.front: When does an ionic compound conduct electricity?
cards.back: When it is **molten or dissolved in water**, because mobile ions carry the charge. A solid ionic compound does not conduct because its ions are not free to move.
cards.hint: Which particles must be able to move?

cards.front: Why are many metals malleable while ionic solids tend to fracture?
cards.back: In metals, **layers of ions can shift** while attraction to the mobile electrons remains. In ionic solids, shifting can bring like-charged ions together, causing repulsion and fracture.
cards.hint: Think about what happens when layers move.
